extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary history; playwrights and critics interested in early-18th-century drama and periodical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for early-18th-century comedy, drama, opera-libretto writing, and periodical social/political prose—drawn from criticism of Addison and Steele. Useful for judging moral tone, dramatic technique, adaptation, and public taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid an overly didactic manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Didactic manner is repugnant; a work that reads like a professional man teaching rules of his own art offends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes of Steele's 'Christian Hero' that 'the book was too didactic' and that 'an air of superiority, freely allowed only to the professional man teaching rules of his own art, belongs to a too didactic manner.' As guidance: moral instruction should not become a sermonizing superiority that repels readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base comedy on seriousness (seriousness as foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each comedy should be based on seriousness; gaiety and humour should rest upon serious thought rather than mere frivolity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page asserts 'Each comedy of his was based on seriousness, as all sound English wit has been...' and that the 'gay manner did not conceal all the earnest thoughts that might jar with the humour of the town.' Practically: humorous surface supported by genuine moral or social concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oaths and unwholesome expletives on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedies should be 'wholly free from the garnish of oaths and unwholesome expletives' which some contemporaries used for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's plays are praised for not relying on coarse language for stage emphasis; this is presented as a moral and aesthetic virtue—cleaner language better serves wit and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend gaiety with earnest thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'gay manner' must not hide earnest ideas; comedy can and should carry serious censures or convictions beneath humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes Steele 'gave unostentatiously a lively wit to the true service of religion' and that humour can coexist with 'the great earnestness of his censure.' Guidance: let laughter carry ethical observation rather than dilute it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let piety/moralizing spoil the art of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive piety or moralizing can move a work beyond comedy into morality-play territory and harm its artistic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steele's 'Lying Lover' was said to have been 'damned for its piety'—his changes made the ending too moral and the piece 'beyond the bounds of comedy.' Practical rule: ensure moral ends do not break dramatic tone or genre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure dramatic 'strokes' are strong enough for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes and character-strokes must be pronounced enough to register to a popular audience at a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele (speaking of Addison's 'Drummer') reports critics who thought 'the strokes were not strong enough to appear at a distance.' For stage-writing, make actions, reactions, and types clearly visible in performance; subtle literary touches may not translate into theatrical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that delicate touches may be lost on popular audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate or subtle humour and detail can escape 'the audience' and be 'too delicate for every taste'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele claimed the 'Drummer' had 'touches being too delicate for every taste in a popular assembly.' Guidance: if targeting a popular stage audience, balance refinement with intelligible, robust comic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations should suit the moral and social temper of the age
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting foreign or classical works, alter endings, emphases, and character treatment to accord with 'a reforming age' and public morals.
